pages.title: What is Artificial Intelligence?
pages.question: What is AI and how does it differ from machine learning?
pages.summary: AI is the broad field of building software that performs tasks we normally associate with human judgement. Machine learning and generative AI are subsets of it.

pages.title: What is Generative AI?
pages.question: What is generative AI and what can it do?
pages.summary: Generative AI models create new content — text, images, audio, video and code — by learning the patterns in very large training sets.

pages.title: What is a Large Language Model (LLM)?
pages.question: What is an LLM and how does it generate text?
pages.summary: A large language model is a neural network trained on vast amounts of text to predict the next token, which lets it write, summarise, translate, reason about text and write code.

pages.title: What are Tokens in AI?
pages.question: What is a token and why do tokens matter for AI cost and limits?
pages.summary: Tokens are the chunks of text — whole words, word pieces or punctuation — that language models read and write. Limits and pricing are usually measured in them.

pages.title: What is a Context Window?
pages.question: What is a context window and why does AI forget things?
pages.summary: The context window is the maximum amount of text, measured in tokens, that a model can consider in a single request. Anything outside it is invisible to the model.

pages.title: What is a Transformer? (Attention Explained)
pages.question: What is the transformer architecture and what does attention do?
pages.summary: The transformer is the neural-network design behind most modern language models. Its key idea, attention, lets every token weigh how relevant every other token is.

pages.title: What is Multimodal AI?
pages.question: What does multimodal AI mean and what can it do?
pages.summary: Multimodal AI models work with more than one type of data — for example text, images, audio and video — in the same system.

pages.title: Prompt Engineering: How to Write Better AI Prompts
pages.question: How do I write effective prompts for AI models?
pages.summary: Prompt engineering is the practice of giving a model clear instructions, context, examples and format requirements so it produces useful, reliable output.
aliases: how do I create better AI prompts

relatedTools.reason: If you want a structure to start from, the AI Prompt Builder walks you through six sections — role, request, context, process, tone and output — and assembles them into a single prompt you can copy into any AI assistant.

pages.title: What is a System Prompt?
pages.question: What is a system prompt and how is it different from a user prompt?
pages.summary: A system prompt is the standing set of instructions that defines how an AI model or assistant should behave, separate from what a user types in each message.

relatedTools.reason: Drafting the role, context, process and output sections of a system prompt is much like filling in the AI Prompt Builder sections. It can help you organise the text, which you then adapt for your application.

pages.title: Common Prompting Mistakes (and How to Fix Them)
pages.question: Why are my AI prompts giving bad answers?
pages.summary: Most poor AI output traces back to a handful of prompt problems: vague goals, missing context, no format, conflicting instructions and no testing.
aliases: why is AI giving wrong answers

relatedTools.reason: Several of these mistakes — missing context, no stated output format, no tone — disappear when each part has its own box. The AI Prompt Builder is one way to check you have filled them in before sending.

pages.title: AI Hallucinations: Why Models Make Things Up
pages.question: What are AI hallucinations and why do they happen?
pages.summary: A hallucination is output that sounds plausible but is false, unsupported or fabricated. It follows from how language models generate text.

pages.summary: You cannot remove hallucinations completely, but you can lower them by grounding answers in sources, constraining the task, allowing "I don't know", and verifying output.

pages.title: What are Embeddings in AI?
pages.question: What is an embedding and how is it used for search?
pages.summary: An embedding is a list of numbers that represents the meaning of a piece of content, so similar meanings end up close together and can be found mathematically.

pages.title: What is a Vector Database?
pages.question: What is a vector database and when do I need one?
pages.summary: A vector database stores embeddings and quickly finds the ones nearest to a query vector, which is the retrieval step in semantic search and RAG.

pages.title: Chunking: How to Split Documents for RAG
pages.question: How should I split documents into chunks for RAG?
pages.summary: Chunking splits long documents into retrievable pieces. Chunk size and boundaries strongly affect whether retrieval finds the right information.

pages.title: What is RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)?
pages.question: What is RAG and how does it work?
pages.summary: Retrieval-Augmented Generation fetches relevant information from your own data and gives it to a language model so answers are grounded in that material.

pages.title: What is Fine-Tuning an AI Model?
pages.question: What is fine-tuning and when is it worth doing?
pages.summary: Fine-tuning continues training a pre-trained model on your own examples so it adopts a consistent behaviour, format or specialised skill.

pages.title: How to Evaluate AI Systems and Outputs
pages.question: How do I test whether my AI system is actually good?
pages.summary: AI evaluation means measuring quality on representative test cases — with automated checks, human review and, carefully, model-based judges — instead of trusting a few good demos.

relatedTools.reason: For one specific evaluation question — "is each claim in this answer supported by the source text?" — the Fact Anchor Checker gives a quick, manual way to compare claims against supplied evidence. It is a spot-check aid

pages.title: What is Local AI? Running Models on Your Own Device
pages.question: Can I run AI models locally on my own computer?
pages.summary: Local AI means running models on hardware you control — a laptop, workstation, server or even in the browser — instead of sending data to a hosted service.

pages.title: AI Privacy and Security: What to Know Before You Paste Data
pages.question: Is it safe to put sensitive data into AI tools?
pages.summary: Using AI safely means controlling what data leaves your environment, understanding provider terms, protecting credentials, and defending applications against manipulation.
aliases: is it safe to paste data into AI

pages.title: What is Prompt Injection?
pages.question: What is prompt injection and how do I defend against it?
pages.summary: Prompt injection is an attack in which text supplied to a model — directly or hidden in documents, web pages or tool results — tries to override the developer's instructions.

pages.title: What are AI Agents?
pages.question: What is an AI agent and how does it work?
pages.summary: An AI agent is a system in which a language model decides what to do next — calling tools, observing results and repeating — to pursue a goal with limited human direction.

pages.title: Agent Tools: How AI Agents Take Actions
pages.question: What are tools in AI agents and how are they designed?
pages.summary: Tools are functions or services a model can ask to be run — search, databases, calculators, APIs, file access — which turn a text generator into something that can act.

pages.title: Function Calling (Tool Calling) Explained
pages.question: What is function calling in LLMs and how does it work?
pages.summary: Function calling lets a model return a structured request to run a named function with arguments, so applications can connect models to code and data reliably.

pages.title: Agent Memory: Short-Term, Long-Term and Beyond
pages.question: How do AI agents remember things?
pages.summary: Models have no built-in memory between requests. Agent memory is whatever your system stores and re-inserts into the context: recent messages, summaries, facts and retrieved knowledge.

pages.title: Multi-Agent Systems Explained
pages.question: What are multi-agent systems and when are they worth it?
pages.summary: A multi-agent system uses several model-driven agents with distinct roles or contexts that coordinate — for example a planner, specialists and a reviewer — to complete a larger task.

pages.title: Agentic Workflows: Patterns for Reliable AI Automation
pages.question: What is an agentic workflow and how is it different from an agent?
pages.summary: An agentic workflow orchestrates model calls and tools along a designed path — chaining, routing, parallelising, evaluating — giving more predictability than a fully autonomous agent.

pages.title: What is MCP (Model Context Protocol)?
pages.question: What is the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and why does it matter?
pages.summary: MCP is an open protocol that standardises how AI applications connect to external tools, data sources and prompts, so one integration can work across many AI clients.

pages.title: MCP Servers and Clients: Roles, Transports and Setup
pages.question: What is the difference between an MCP server, an MCP client and an MCP host?
pages.summary: In MCP, a host application runs clients that each connect to a server; servers expose tools, resources and prompts over a transport such as stdio or HTTP.

pages.title: RAG vs Fine-Tuning: Which Should You Use?
pages.question: Should I use RAG or fine-tuning to customise an LLM?
pages.summary: RAG gives a model access to information at question time; fine-tuning changes the model's behaviour through additional training. They solve different problems and are often combined.

pages.title: AI Agent vs Chatbot vs Assistant: What's the Difference?
pages.question: What is the difference between an AI agent, a chatbot and an AI assistant?
pages.summary: The terms overlap and are used loosely. The practical difference is how much the system can do on its own: converse, help with tasks on request, or pursue goals using tools in a loop.

pages.title: MCP vs API: What's the Difference?
pages.question: How is MCP different from a regular API?
pages.summary: An API is an interface to one service for programmers. MCP is a standard protocol for AI applications to discover and use capabilities, and MCP servers often wrap APIs.

pages.title: Vector Database vs Traditional Database
pages.question: When do I need a vector database instead of SQL or another traditional database?
pages.summary: Traditional databases answer exact, structured questions; vector databases answer "most similar" questions over embeddings. Many systems need both, and some databases do both.
aliases: do I need a vector database

pages.title: Local AI vs Cloud AI: Privacy, Cost, Capability
pages.question: Should I run AI locally or use a cloud AI service?
pages.summary: Local AI keeps data on your device and avoids per-use fees but is limited by your hardware; cloud AI gives access to the most capable models with no setup but means sending data to a provider.

pages.title: Function Calling vs MCP
pages.question: What is the difference between function calling and MCP?
pages.summary: Function calling is a model-API feature for requesting structured calls to functions you define. MCP is a protocol for packaging, sharing and discovering tools across AI applications. They work together.
aliases: difference between MCP and tool use

pages.title: Python for AI: When and How to Use It
pages.question: When should I use Python for AI work?
pages.summary: Python is the most common language for calling models, preparing data, running small RAG pipelines and evaluating answers. Use it when you want clear scripts and a rich library ecosystem; keep secrets and long-running work on a machine you control.
aliases: when to use python for AI
python machine learning basics for apps

pages.title: Building RAG with Python
pages.question: How do I build RAG with Python?
pages.summary: Build retrieval-augmented generation in Python by loading documents, chunking them, embedding chunks, storing vectors, retrieving neighbours for a question, stuffing them into a prompt, and checking the answer.
aliases: How do I build RAG with Python?

pages.title: Calling AI and Model APIs with Python
pages.question: How do I call a model API from Python?
pages.summary: Call a model from Python with an HTTP request: read the API key from the environment, set a timeout, send a JSON body, handle errors, and pull the text out of the response.
aliases: how to call an LLM from python

pages.title: JSON and CSV Handling for AI Work in Python
pages.question: How do I handle JSON and CSV data for AI pipelines in Python?
pages.summary: Read JSON and CSV files in Python, validate the shape you expect, send clean records to a model or embedding API, and save outputs in a format the next step can load.

pages.title: Python AI Libraries: What to Use When
pages.question: Which Python libraries should I use for AI applications?
pages.summary: Choose Python libraries by role: standard library and an HTTP client for API calls, a data library for tables, an embeddings or vector helper for retrieval, and an agent framework only when orchestration outgrows a simple loop.

pages.title: JavaScript for AI Applications
pages.question: How do I use JavaScript for AI applications?
pages.summary: Use JavaScript for AI UIs in the browser and for server-side calls in Node. Never put model API keys in front-end code; call your own backend, which holds the secret and talks to the model.

pages.title: TypeScript for AI Applications
pages.question: Why use TypeScript for AI applications?
pages.summary: TypeScript adds types to JavaScript so request and response shapes for model APIs and your own backend stay consistent, catching many integration bugs before runtime.

pages.title: TypeScript Types for an API Client
pages.question: How do I write TypeScript types for an API client?
pages.summary: Define TypeScript types for the request body, success response and error response of each API call, then implement a client function that returns a typed result and handles non-2xx cases.
aliases: TypeScript types for an API client

pages.title: Calling AI Services from JavaScript and TypeScript
pages.question: How do I call AI services from JavaScript or TypeScript?
pages.summary: From Node (or another server), call the model vendor with fetch, an API key from the environment, timeouts and careful JSON parsing. Expose only your own authenticated route to browsers.

pages.title: Streaming AI Responses for Chat UIs
pages.question: What is streaming for AI chat responses and how does a client read it?
pages.summary: Streaming delivers model tokens as they are generated (often SSE or chunked HTTP) so the UI can show text immediately. The client reads the byte stream, parses events, and appends text until the stream ends.

pages.title: Building AI Interfaces with React
pages.question: How do I build an AI chat interface in React?
pages.summary: Build a React chat UI with a message list, an input box, loading and error states, and calls to your backend — never with a model API key in the client bundle.

pages.title: Chatbot State and Conversation UI in React
pages.question: How should I manage React state for a chatbot?
pages.summary: Model chatbot state as a messages array with roles, a pending flag, and optional streaming buffers. Keep the API key off the client and treat each turn as append-only history you send to your backend.

pages.title: Node.js for AI Applications
pages.question: How do I use Node.js for AI applications?
pages.summary: Use Node.js as the server that holds API keys, authenticates users, calls the model vendor, and exposes a thin route your React (or other) client can call.

pages.title: Streaming AI Responses with Node.js
pages.question: How do I stream AI responses with Node.js from an API?
pages.summary: In Node.js, call the vendor streaming endpoint, then forward chunks to the browser as SSE or chunked HTTP while handling backpressure, aborts and errors.
aliases: Node.js streaming responses from an API

pages.title: What is an AI Framework?
pages.question: What is an AI framework?
pages.summary: An AI framework is a library that helps you orchestrate prompts, tools, memory and model calls. It sits above the raw HTTP API and below your product logic — unlike the model itself.

pages.title: How to Choose an Agent Framework
pages.question: Which framework can I use for an AI agent?
pages.summary: Choose an agent approach by category: direct API loops, prompt/orchestration helpers, tool-calling loops, multi-agent graphs, or vendor SDKs. Named libraries illustrate categories; pick based on needs, and know when a framework is unnecessary.
aliases: Which framework can I use for an AI agent?
how to choose an agent framework

pages.title: AI Framework vs Direct Model API
pages.question: Should I use an AI framework or call the model API directly?
pages.summary: Call the model API directly when the flow is simple and you want full visibility; use a framework when shared orchestration, tools or retrieval abstractions clearly reduce risk and duplication.

pages.title: Databases for AI Applications
pages.question: What database fundamentals do AI applications need?
pages.summary: AI apps still need ordinary databases for users, conversations, documents and evaluation rows. Vectors are an extra index for similarity — not a replacement for relational data.

pages.title: Using PostgreSQL in AI Applications
pages.question: How do I use PostgreSQL with my app when it includes AI features?
pages.summary: Use PostgreSQL to store users, chats and documents with parameterised queries; call the model from your app server; add pgvector later only if you need similarity search in the same database.
aliases: How do I use PostgreSQL with my app?

pages.title: Connecting AI Agents to External Applications
pages.question: How do AI agents connect to external applications?
pages.summary: An agent reaches Gmail, calendars or CRMs only through tools you define and run. The model requests a tool call; your server performs the API or MCP action with proper credentials and permissions.

pages.title: Gmail and Google Integration for AI Agents
pages.question: How can an AI agent access Gmail?
pages.summary: An agent accesses Gmail through your server: the user completes Google OAuth, you store a refresh token, and a tool lists or drafts mail via the Gmail API. IntelliTools has no Gmail connector; treat message text as untrusted.
aliases: How can an AI agent access Gmail?

pages.title: OAuth for AI Agents
pages.question: How does OAuth work for AI agents?
pages.summary: OAuth lets a user grant your agent app limited access to a provider without sharing their password. Your server holds tokens; the model only triggers tools that use those tokens under your policy.

pages.title: Permissions and Security for AI Integrations
pages.question: What permissions and security practices should AI integrations use?
pages.summary: Limit OAuth scopes, enforce authorisation in code, require human approval before send or delete, and treat tool outputs such as email bodies as untrusted to reduce prompt injection and data leaks.

pages.title: JSON Fundamentals for API Work
pages.question: What is JSON and how is it used in APIs?
pages.summary: JSON is a text format for structured data — objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans and null — used by almost every modern HTTP API and by model tool arguments.

pages.title: How to Validate JSON
pages.question: How do I validate JSON before I trust it?
pages.summary: Validate JSON by parsing it safely, then checking required fields, types and allowed values — ideally with a schema. Reject unexpected shapes before they reach your model or database.

pages.title: What is an API?
pages.question: What is an API in practice?
pages.summary: An API is how one program asks another program to do work or return data — commonly over HTTP with JSON. Model providers expose APIs; your app exposes APIs to your own UI.

pages.title: REST APIs for Application Development
pages.question: What is a REST API and how do I use one?
pages.summary: REST APIs expose resources over HTTP using methods like GET, POST, PUT and DELETE, usually with JSON bodies and status codes that tell you whether the call worked.

pages.title: API Authentication: Keys, Sessions and OAuth
pages.question: How should APIs authenticate clients?
pages.summary: Choose API keys for server-to-server access, session cookies for browser users, and OAuth when acting on a user's behalf at another provider. Always keep secrets on the server.

pages.title: What is SharePoint?
pages.question: What is SharePoint and when do teams use it?
pages.summary: SharePoint is Microsoft's platform for team sites, document libraries, pages and intranet content inside Microsoft 365. Custom UI on modern pages is built with the SharePoint Framework, not classic farm solutions.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: SharePoint Framework (SPFx)
pages.question: What is SPFx?
pages.summary: SPFx is the SharePoint Framework: Microsoft's TypeScript toolchain for client-side SharePoint web parts and extensions. The default UI library is React, and projects are TypeScript-first.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: How to Build an SPFx Web Part
pages.question: How do I build an SPFx web part?
pages.summary: Build an SPFx web part by scaffolding a React and TypeScript project with the SharePoint generator, coding against the web part context, serving the workbench, then packaging an .sppkg for the app catalog.
aliases: How do I build an SPFx web part?
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Microsoft 365 for Developers
pages.question: What is Microsoft 365 and what does M365 include?
pages.summary: Microsoft 365 (M365) is the cloud suite that includes SharePoint, Exchange, Teams and the identity boundary in Entra ID. Developers extend it with Graph, SPFx and Teams apps rather than scraping the web UI.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Microsoft Graph API
pages.question: What is the Microsoft Graph API and how do I call it?
pages.summary: Microsoft Graph is the REST API for Microsoft 365: users, groups, mail, files, sites, calendars and Teams. You call https://graph.microsoft.com with an Entra ID access token and the scopes an admin has consented.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Power Platform Basics
pages.question: What is the Power Platform and when should developers use it?
pages.summary: Power Platform is Microsoft's low-code family: Power Apps for UI, Power Automate for workflows, Power BI for reports, and Dataverse for data, sitting beside Microsoft 365 and Azure rather than replacing them.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Microsoft Entra ID
pages.question: What is Microsoft Entra ID?
pages.summary: Microsoft Entra ID is Microsoft's cloud identity service, formerly Azure Active Directory. It signs users in, issues tokens, and holds the app registrations that Microsoft Graph, Azure and your own apps trust.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Microsoft Teams Development
pages.question: How do I build an app for Microsoft Teams?
pages.summary: Teams apps are packages of tabs, bots, message extensions and connectors that run inside Microsoft Teams and usually call Microsoft Graph. They are not SPFx web parts, though a tab can host a web app or an SPFx part.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Azure Fundamentals for Application Developers
pages.question: What is Microsoft Azure and which services matter for an app?
pages.summary: Azure is Microsoft's cloud for compute, data, identity integration and AI hosting. Application teams usually start with App Service or containers, a database, storage, Key Vault and Entra ID, not with every service in the catalog.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Hugging Face for Builders
pages.question: What is Hugging Face and when do I use it?
pages.summary: Hugging Face is the common hub for open model weights, datasets and libraries such as transformers and the Hub. Teams use it to find models, download weights, and sometimes to host inference, then decide what must run in their own environment.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: LangChain, Practically
pages.question: What is LangChain and when should I use it?
pages.summary: LangChain is a Python and JavaScript framework that wires prompts, models, tools and retrieval into chains or agents. It speeds prototypes and adds abstraction; simple apps are often clearer calling a model API directly.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: LlamaIndex for Retrieval
pages.question: What is LlamaIndex and how is it different from LangChain?
pages.summary: LlamaIndex is a framework focused on loading data, building indexes and retrieving context for language models. It overlaps LangChain on RAG, with more emphasis on document indices and less on being a general agent toolkit.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Model APIs for Applications
pages.question: What is a model API and how should I call one?
pages.summary: A model API is an HTTP service that accepts messages and returns generated text or tool calls. You choose a model, send a prompt with authentication, handle tokens and errors, and keep the vendor SDK or raw HTTP behind a small interface you own.
aliases: how do I call an LLM API
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Local LLM Runtimes
pages.question: What are Ollama, llama.cpp and vLLM?
pages.summary: Local LLM runtimes such as Ollama, llama.cpp and vLLM load open weights on hardware you control and often expose an HTTP API. They trade operational work and hardware limits for privacy and a predictable machine.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: RAG Frameworks
pages.question: What is a RAG framework and do I need one?
pages.summary: A RAG framework packages document loading, chunking, embeddings, retrieval and prompting. LlamaIndex and LangChain are the usual examples. Use one for speed; drop to plain code when you need to see every step.
aliases: do I need a RAG framework
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: AI SDKs
pages.question: What is an AI SDK and how is it different from a model API?
pages.summary: An AI SDK is a library that calls a model API for you: authentication, types, streaming and retries. The Vercel AI SDK, official provider SDKs and similar toolkits are convenience layers. Your architecture is still the HTTP contract and your own wrapper.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Python
pages.question: What is Python and when should I use it?
pages.summary: Python is a readable general-purpose language with a huge library ecosystem. It dominates data work, scripting and many AI prototypes, and it is a solid choice for backends when raw latency is not the main constraint.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: JavaScript
pages.question: What is JavaScript?
pages.summary: JavaScript is the language of web browsers and, with Node.js, a server language too. It is dynamically typed, event-driven, and the base that TypeScript compiles to. JS is the everyday abbreviation.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: TypeScript
pages.question: What is TypeScript?
pages.summary: TypeScript (TS) is JavaScript with a static type system. It compiles to plain JavaScript, catches a class of bugs in the editor, and is the default for SPFx, large React apps and many Node services.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Java
pages.question: What is Java and when is it the right language?
pages.summary: Java is a statically typed, object-oriented language that runs on the JVM. Enterprises use it for long-lived services, Android's older stacks, and anywhere a stable toolchain and explicit types matter more than a short script.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: C#
pages.question: What is C# and when do teams choose it?
pages.summary: C# is Microsoft's typed language on .NET. Teams use it for Windows services, cross-platform web APIs, Unity games, and Azure backends. It is a strong default when the stack is already Microsoft.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: The Go Programming Language
pages.question: What is the Go programming language?
pages.summary: Go (Golang) is a small, statically typed language designed for simple concurrent services and single-binary deployments. Teams pick it for APIs, CLIs and infrastructure tools when they want fast builds and boring code.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Rust
pages.question: What is Rust and when is it worth the learning cost?
pages.summary: Rust is a systems language with ownership and borrowing instead of a garbage collector. It prevents many memory bugs at compile time. Teams use it for performance-critical tools, WASM, and services where correctness matters more than a short compile.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: SQL
pages.question: What is SQL and how do I use it well?
pages.summary: SQL is the language of relational databases: you declare tables and ask questions with SELECT, JOIN, and WHERE. ORMs can generate SQL, but you still need to read it to understand performance and correctness.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: HTML and CSS
pages.question: What are HTML and CSS?
pages.summary: HTML is the structure of a web page. CSS is how that structure looks. JavaScript changes behaviour. You need the first two even when a framework such as React writes them for you.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: React
pages.question: What is React?
pages.summary: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces out of components that render when state changes. It is the usual UI layer in SPFx and in many AI chat panels, but it is not a backend or a complete framework.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Next.js
pages.question: What is Next.js and when should I use it?
pages.summary: Next.js is a React framework that adds routing, server rendering, and server-side code next to the UI. Use it for full web apps. Use plain React when you only need a widget inside someone else's page.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Node.js
pages.question: What is Node.js?
pages.summary: Node.js is a JavaScript runtime outside the browser, used for servers, tools and scripts. It is built on V8 and an event loop, and it is the usual host for Express, Next.js servers, and SPFx build tooling.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Express
pages.question: What is Express.js?
pages.summary: Express is a small Node.js library for HTTP servers: routes, middleware, and request and response objects. It is enough for many APIs. It does not include a database, auth, or a front end.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Frontend and Backend
pages.question: What is the difference between frontend and backend?
pages.summary: The frontend is the interface running on the user's device. The backend is the server you control: data, secrets, and business rules. Browsers are not a safe place for secrets, which is why AI keys and database passwords stay on the backend.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: GraphQL
pages.question: What is GraphQL and how is it different from REST?
pages.summary: GraphQL is an API style where the client sends a query that names the fields it wants, and the server resolves them against a schema. It reduces over-fetching and adds a different set of caching, auth and performance problems than REST.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: WebSockets
pages.question: What are WebSockets and when should I use them?
pages.summary: WebSockets are a persistent two-way connection between a client and a server, used for live updates. They are more machinery than HTTP request and response. Many AI chat UIs only need server-sent events, not a full socket.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: REST versus GraphQL
pages.question: Should I use REST or GraphQL?
pages.summary: REST exposes resources over HTTP verbs and status codes. GraphQL exposes a schema and lets the client name fields. REST is the default for most services. GraphQL pays off when many clients need different shapes of the same data.
aliases: REST or GraphQL for my API
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: PostgreSQL, the Relational Database
pages.question: What is PostgreSQL?
pages.summary: PostgreSQL (Postgres, often shortened to PG) is an open-source relational database. It stores tables with constraints, speaks SQL, and can add extensions such as pgvector. It is a strong default system of record for applications.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: MySQL
pages.question: What is MySQL and how does it differ from PostgreSQL?
pages.summary: MySQL is a widely used open-source relational database, common in existing web stacks and managed as Aurora or Cloud SQL. It speaks SQL with its own dialect and defaults. Pick it to extend a MySQL estate; pick PostgreSQL for many new apps unless your platform is already MySQL.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: SQLite
pages.question: What is SQLite and when is a single file enough?
pages.summary: SQLite is a relational database stored in one file inside your process. It is the right default for local tools, tests, mobile apps and modest servers. It is the wrong default for many writers across many application servers.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: MongoDB
pages.question: What is MongoDB and when is a document database right?
pages.summary: MongoDB is a document database: you store JSON-like documents in collections and query them by fields. It fits data you mostly load as a whole document. It is a poor replacement for relational constraints you actually need.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Redis
pages.question: What is Redis and when should an application use it?
pages.summary: Redis is an in-memory data store for keys with a few rich values: strings, lists, sets, sorted sets, and expirations. Applications use it for cache, rate limits, short-lived sessions and queues, not as the only copy of data they cannot lose.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: ORMs and Prisma
pages.question: What is an ORM and when should I use Prisma?
pages.summary: An ORM maps database rows to objects in your language. Prisma is a popular TypeScript ORM that generates a client from a schema file. ORMs speed ordinary queries and can hide the SQL that explains a slow page.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Choosing a Vector Store
pages.question: Which vector database should I use?
pages.summary: Choose a vector store by how you already run data: pgvector inside PostgreSQL, a dedicated vector database, or an in-process library for small sets. The retrieval quality depends more on chunking and embeddings than on the brand.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: SQL versus NoSQL
pages.question: Should I use SQL or NoSQL?
pages.summary: SQL databases store related rows with constraints. NoSQL is a loose label for documents, key-value stores and others. Choose based on access patterns and the invariants you need, not on which word sounds newer.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Git
pages.question: What is Git and how should a team use it?
pages.summary: Git is a distributed version-control system. It records snapshots of a project so you can branch, review, and return to a known state. GitHub is a host for Git repositories, not the tool itself.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: GitHub
pages.question: What is GitHub and how is it different from Git?
pages.summary: GitHub is a website and service that hosts Git repositories and adds pull requests, issues, actions and access control. Git is the tool. GitHub is one place teams push Git history and review it.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Docker
pages.question: What is Docker and when should I containerise an app?
pages.summary: Docker is a tool for building and running containers: a packaged process with its filesystem. Use it to make local and production environments match. Do not use it to hide a broken build, and do not run everything as root.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Containers
pages.question: What is a container and how is it different from a virtual machine?
pages.summary: A container is a process, or a small group of processes, isolated with its own filesystem view, using the host kernel. A virtual machine emulates a whole computer and boots its own kernel. Containers are the usual way to ship a service.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: CI and CD
pages.question: What is CI/CD?
pages.summary: Continuous integration automatically builds and tests every change. Continuous delivery prepares a deployable artifact; continuous deployment ships it. The point is a repeatable pipeline, not a YAML file that nobody trusts.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Environment Variables
pages.question: What are environment variables and where should secrets live?
pages.summary: Environment variables are named strings a process inherits from whoever started it. They are the standard way to configure an app per environment. Secrets can live there at runtime, but they must not live in git, images, or client bundles.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Package Managers
pages.question: What is a package manager and why do lockfiles matter?
pages.summary: A package manager installs libraries and records versions. npm, pip, Cargo and NuGet are examples. A lockfile pins the tree so tomorrow's install matches today's. Installing global packages at random is how machines drift.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: AWS Fundamentals for Application Developers
pages.question: What is AWS and which services matter for an app?
pages.summary: Amazon Web Services is a cloud platform: compute, storage, databases and managed APIs in regions and accounts. Most new apps need a place to run, a database, object storage, identity and logs, not the full catalog.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Google Cloud Fundamentals for Application Developers
pages.question: What is Google Cloud and which services matter for an app?
pages.summary: Google Cloud (GCP) is a public cloud organised into projects. Application teams usually need Cloud Run or another compute option, a database, Cloud Storage, IAM, and logs. BigQuery and Vertex are optional, not the starting point.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: OAuth 2.0
pages.question: What is OAuth and when do I use it?
pages.summary: OAuth 2.0 is a protocol for granting a client limited access to an API without sharing the user's password. It is how sign-in buttons and Microsoft Graph access tokens usually start. It is not itself a login profile; OpenID Connect adds identity on top.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: OpenID Connect
pages.question: What is OpenID Connect and how is it different from OAuth?
pages.summary: OpenID Connect (OIDC) is a thin identity layer on OAuth 2.0. It gives your app an ID token that says who signed in. OAuth alone gives an access token for an API. Most sign-in-with buttons are OIDC.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: JSON Web Tokens
pages.question: What is a JWT and how do I validate one?
pages.summary: A JWT is a signed JSON payload used as a token. Anyone can read the payload. Only a valid signature, the right issuer and the right audience make it trustworthy. Decoding is not validation.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: API Keys
pages.question: What is an API key and how should I store one?
pages.summary: An API key is a secret string that identifies a caller to an API. It is simple and blunt: anyone who has it is the caller. Keep keys on the server, scope them, rotate them, and do not ship them in a browser or a mobile binary.
aliases: where to store an API key
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Authentication versus Authorization
pages.question: What is the difference between authentication and authorization?
pages.summary: Authentication answers who is calling. Authorization answers what they may do. A valid login is not permission to read every row. Check both, on the server, for every action that matters.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: CORS
pages.question: What is CORS and why does the browser block my API?
pages.summary: CORS is a browser rule for cross-origin requests. The server must opt in with response headers. It is not authentication, and it is not a barrier to non-browser clients. Fix it by allowing the origins you intend, not by reflecting every origin with credentials.
aliases: why is my API blocked by CORS
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Webhooks
pages.question: What is a webhook and how do I handle one safely?
pages.summary: A webhook is an HTTP callback: another system POSTs to your URL when something happens. You must authenticate the sender, respond quickly, and process the event idempotently. A public URL with no signature check is an unauthenticated API.
headings: Why and when it is used

pages.title: Test-Time Compute (Inference-Time Scaling)

pages.summary: Test-time compute means spending more computation when a model answers — longer reasoning, several attempts, search or verification — instead of only making the model bigger.

Is it better to use a bigger model or more inference compute

pages.summary: Attention sinks are the first few tokens of a sequence that transformers attend to heavily even when they carry little meaning. StreamingLLM keeps those tokens plus a recent window in the KV cache so a model can stream indefinitely without collapsing.
aliases: Why does sliding window attention break when the first tokens are dropped
How many sink tokens does StreamingLLM keep

pages.title: FlashAttention-3 (and FlashAttention-4)
pages.question: What is FlashAttention-3?
pages.summary: FlashAttention-3 is an exact attention implementation redesigned for NVIDIA Hopper GPUs. It overlaps data movement and computation, interleaves matrix multiplication with softmax, and uses FP8 low-precision, reaching up to about 740 TFLOPs/s in FP16 on H100.
aliases: How is FlashAttention-3 different from FlashAttention-2
Does FlashAttention-3 work on A100 GPUs

glossary.definition: A system in which a model pursues a goal by repeatedly choosing actions, calling tools and reading the results until it finishes or hits a limit.
A designed process that combines model calls, tools, checks and sometimes humans along a path the developer defines, as opposed to a model freely choosing every step.
The broad field of building software that performs tasks normally associated with human judgement, such as perception, language and decision-making.
Work to make AI systems behave in line with human intentions and values, including being helpful, honest and safe. Training steps such as instruction tuning and preference tuning contribute to it.
A family of search methods that quickly find vectors that are very likely, though not guaranteed, to be the closest to a query. Used by vector databases to stay fast at scale.
The mechanism in a transformer that lets each token weigh how relevant every other token is when building its representation.
A standard test used to compare models on a defined task. Useful for rough comparison, but not a substitute for testing on your own use case.
A prompting technique in which the model is encouraged to work through intermediate reasoning steps before giving its answer. Its usefulness varies by model and task.
Software that converses with users. Modern chatbots are usually powered by LLMs; the word says little about whether the system can take actions.
Splitting documents into smaller passages so each can be embedded and retrieved on its own, as in RAG.
The maximum amount of text, measured in tokens, a model can consider in one request, covering instructions, conversation, documents and the reply.
A measure of how closely two vectors point in the same direction. It is widely used to compare embeddings: values near 1 mean very similar, near 0 mean unrelated.
Machine learning that uses neural networks with many layers. It underlies most modern vision, speech and language models.
A generative model, common in image generation, that starts from random noise and refines it step by step into content matching a prompt.
A list of numbers (a vector) that represents the meaning of content so that similar items are close together. Basis of semantic search and RAG.
Structured tests that measure how well an AI system performs on tasks you care about, using test cases, graders and tracked scores.
Including a small number of example inputs and outputs in the prompt to show the model the pattern you want. Zero-shot means giving no examples.
Further training a pre-trained model on your own examples so it adopts a consistent behaviour, format or skill.
A large model trained on broad data that can be adapted to many tasks. Large language models are the best-known example.
A model-API feature in which the model returns a structured request to run a named function with arguments. Your code runs it and returns the result.
AI that produces new content such as text, images, audio, video or code.
Tying a model's answer to supplied source material or tool results so claims can be traced and checked.
Checks and limits around an AI system, such as input filters, output validation, permission limits and human approvals, that reduce harmful or unwanted behaviour.
Fluent, confident model output that is false, unsupported by the sources, or invented, such as fake citations or facts.
A design in which a person reviews or approves AI output or actions at defined points, especially before high-impact or irreversible steps.
Combining keyword search with vector similarity (often plus metadata filters), so exact terms and meaning are both covered.
Running a trained model to produce output for new input, as opposed to training it.
Additional training that teaches a pre-trained model to follow instructions and respond helpfully, turning a text predictor into an assistant.
An attempt to get a model to break its safety rules through crafted input. Related to, but distinct from, prompt injection.
The point after which a model's training data contains no information. Later events are unknown to it unless supplied via the prompt, search or tools.
A very large neural network trained on text to predict the next token, enabling writing, summarising, translation, question answering and code generation.
Running models on hardware you control instead of a hosted service, so data need not leave your device.
A parameter-efficient fine-tuning method that trains small add-on matrices while the original model stays frozen, greatly reducing training cost.
The part of AI in which systems learn patterns from data rather than following hand-written rules.
An open protocol for connecting AI applications to external tools, data and prompts through servers that clients can discover and call.
The component inside an AI host application that holds a connection to one MCP server and relays requests and results.
A program that exposes tools, resources and prompts to MCP clients, often wrapping an existing API, database or file system.
Information a system stores outside the model and re-inserts into the prompt, such as recent messages, summaries and durable facts, because models themselves retain nothing between requests.
A setup in which several model-driven agents with distinct roles or contexts cooperate on a larger task.
Able to handle more than one type of data, such as text together with images or audio.
A model made of layers of simple connected units whose strengths (parameters) are adjusted during training. The basis of deep learning.
Models whose trained parameters are published for download and local use, subject to the licence. Not always the same as fully open source.
When a model or prompt works well on the examples used to build it but poorly on new cases. Held-out test data helps detect it.
The numbers inside a model that are adjusted during training and determine its behaviour. Model size is often quoted as a parameter count.
The initial, large-scale training stage in which a model learns general patterns from broad data before any specialised adaptation.
The input given to a model: instructions, context, examples and the user's request.
An attack where text supplied to a model, directly or hidden in content it reads, tries to override the developer's instructions.
Storing a model's parameters at lower numeric precision to cut memory use, usually at some cost in quality.
Retrieving relevant passages from your data and giving them to a model so its answer is based on that material.
A second, more precise scoring step that reorders retrieved candidates before they are given to the model.
A training approach that uses human preference judgements to steer a model towards responses people rate as better.
The step where the next token is chosen from the model's probabilities. Settings such as temperature control how predictable or varied the choice is.
Searching by meaning rather than exact words, usually by comparing embeddings.
Model output constrained to a defined format, such as JSON matching a schema, so software can use it directly.
Standing instructions from the developer that define a model's role, rules and format across a conversation, separate from the user's messages.
A setting that controls randomness when a model picks the next token. Lower values give more predictable output; higher values give more varied output.
The unit of text a model reads and writes: a word, part of a word, or punctuation. Limits and prices are commonly measured in tokens.
The component that splits text into tokens and maps them to numbers. Different model families use different tokenizers.
A described capability, such as search, a database query or an API call, that a model can request and that your code executes.
The process of adjusting a model's parameters using data so its outputs improve on a target task.
The neural-network architecture, introduced in 2017, behind most modern language models. Its key feature is attention.
An ordered list of numbers. In AI, embeddings are vectors, and closeness between vectors reflects similarity in meaning.
A system that stores embedding vectors with metadata and finds the closest matches to a query vector quickly.
Asking a model to perform a task with instructions only and no examples.
A secret string a program sends to an API to identify itself. Anyone who has the key can call the API as that program, so it belongs on a server, not in a browser.
The usual OAuth 2.0 flow for user login: the browser gets a short-lived code, and the server exchanges that code for tokens. Public clients add PKCE so a stolen code is not enough.
A statically typed language on .NET, commonly used for APIs, workers and Azure services in Microsoft-centred stacks.
A process isolated with its own filesystem view, built from an image and run by a container runtime. It shares the host kernel, unlike a virtual machine.
A browser check that asks a server whether a page from another origin may read the response. It is not authentication, and non-browser clients ignore it.
Microsoft's cloud identity service, formerly Azure Active Directory. It signs users in and issues tokens for Microsoft 365, Azure and registered apps.
A small Node.js library for HTTP routes and middleware. It does not include a database or a front end.
A distributed version-control system that records snapshots of a project so you can branch, merge and recover history.
An API style in which the client names the fields it wants and the server resolves them against a schema. Not the same thing as Microsoft Graph.
A hub and set of libraries for publishing and loading machine-learning models and datasets, including the transformers library.
A signed token whose payload is JSON. The payload is readable by anyone; trust comes only from checking the signature, issuer, audience and expiry.
A framework for composing model calls, tools and retrieval in Python or JavaScript. It is optional glue, not a model.
A framework focused on loading documents, indexing them and retrieving context for a language model.
Microsoft's cloud suite for mail, files, SharePoint and Teams. Office 365 is the older name for the same tenant story.
The REST API at graph.microsoft.com for Microsoft 365 data such as users, mail, files, sites and Teams. It is not GraphQL.
A React framework that adds routing and a server runtime so secrets and data fetching can stay off the browser.
A protocol for granting an application limited access to an API without sharing the user's password. OpenID Connect adds sign-in identity on top.
An identity layer on OAuth 2.0. The ID token says who signed in. The access token is what you send to an API.
A library that maps database rows to objects in a programming language. Prisma is one TypeScript example. The SQL still runs.
An open-source relational database. Applications talk to it with SQL. The pgvector extension can store embeddings in the same server.
Microsoft's low-code family: Power Apps, Power Automate, Power BI and Dataverse, used for tenant workflows beside Microsoft 365.
An in-memory store for keys, expirations, counters and short-lived coordination. Best used as a cache or rate limiter beside a durable database.
Microsoft 365's platform for sites, document libraries, lists and intranet pages. Modern custom web parts are built with the SharePoint Framework.
Microsoft's TypeScript toolchain for client-side SharePoint web parts and extensions. The usual UI library is React.
The short name for the SharePoint Framework, used to build client-side SharePoint web parts and extensions with TypeScript, usually with React.
JavaScript with a static type system. The compiler emits plain JavaScript. SharePoint Framework projects are TypeScript-first.
An HTTP callback: another system POSTs to your URL when an event happens. Verify the signature and treat retries as normal.

An open protocol for communication between independent AI agents: discovering capabilities, delegating tasks and returning results. It complements MCP, which connects agents to tools. Details are version-dependent.
Generating several candidate answers and returning the one a scorer — tests, a verifier or a reward model — rates highest.
Restricting a model's next-token choices at each step so output must follow a schema, regex or grammar. It guarantees well-formed output, not correct content.
A training approach in which a model critiques and revises its outputs against written principles, with AI-generated preference labels (RLAIF) used for further training.
Curating everything a model sees each turn — instructions, retrieved facts, memory, tool definitions and results — so agents stay reliable.
Training that pulls matching pairs (such as an image and its caption) together in embedding space and pushes non-matching pairs apart. CLIP is a well-known example.

A preference-optimization method that tunes a model directly on chosen-versus-rejected response pairs relative to a reference model, without a separate reward model or RL loop. It is an alignment technique, not ordinary reinforcement learning.
Training a smaller student model to imitate a larger teacher model's outputs, yielding a cheaper model for narrower tasks.
AI that perceives and acts in the physical or simulated world through a body such as a robot arm, drone or vehicle.
An exact attention algorithm that tiles computation to cut memory traffic, speeding up transformers and enabling longer sequences without approximating the result.
A PPO-style reinforcement-learning method that normalises rewards within a group of sampled outputs per prompt, avoiding a separate value model. Used for training on tasks with verifiable rewards.
A model file format used by llama.cpp, supporting many quantisation levels and bundling metadata for local inference.
A neural network that learns on graph-structured data by passing messages between connected nodes, used for molecules, networks and some weather models.
Retrieval that builds a graph of entities and relationships (often with community summaries) so questions needing connections or corpus-wide synthesis can be answered.
Stored attention keys and values for earlier tokens, reused during generation to avoid recomputation. It speeds decoding but grows with context length and batch size.
Using a language model to grade or compare other outputs against a rubric. It scales evaluation but has biases and needs calibration against human judgement.
A model design with many specialist sub-networks and a router that activates only a few per token, so total parameters exceed active parameters.
A structured document describing a model's intended use, training data, evaluation, limitations and ethical considerations.
Degradation of a deployed model's performance as input data or the relationship between inputs and outcomes changes over time.
A multiple-choice benchmark across 57 subjects used to compare breadth of knowledge in language models; now close to saturated for top models.
A scorer that judges only the final answer of a reasoning attempt. Not to be confused with an object-relational mapper in software.
A language-modelling metric reflecting how well a model predicts text; lower means less "surprised". It is not a measure of usefulness or truth.
Information added so a transformer knows token order; methods include sinusoidal encodings, RoPE and ALiBi.
A widely used reinforcement-learning algorithm that clips policy updates to keep training stable; used in RLHF pipelines.
A scorer that rates each intermediate step of a reasoning chain, enabling step-level feedback and guided search.
The family of methods that tune models using comparisons of better versus worse responses — RLHF, DPO, KTO, IPO, ORPO, SimPO and relatives.
Reusing computation for a repeated prompt prefix to cut latency and often cost. Rules and pricing are provider-specific.
A language model trained or configured to work through a problem in intermediate steps before answering, trading latency and cost for accuracy on multi-step tasks.
Structured adversarial testing of an AI system to find failures, misuse paths and vulnerabilities before real attackers or users do.
When a system exploits flaws in its reward signal, scoring highly without doing what was intended.
Training with preference labels generated by an AI model, guided by written principles, instead of human labels.
Reinforcement learning where rewards come from automatic checkers such as exact answer match or unit tests, used to train reasoning behaviour.
Empirical relationships showing how model loss tends to improve predictably with parameters, data and compute.
Sampling several reasoning attempts and choosing the final answer most of them agree on.
A compact language model, typically up to a few billion parameters, that runs cheaply and can be strong on narrow tasks.
Speeding up generation by letting a small draft model propose tokens that a large model verifies in parallel, preserving the large model's output distribution.
A sequence model that carries a compact recurrent state, giving linear-time processing as an alternative to attention; Mamba is a well-known example.
A model's tendency to tell users what they want to hear — agreeing with mistaken claims or flattering them — rather than what is accurate.
Spending extra computation when answering — longer reasoning, multiple samples, search or verification — to improve hard answers.
A provider setting that caps or tunes how much reasoning a model does per request. Names and semantics vary by provider.
A transformer that splits an image into patches treated as tokens, matching or beating CNNs at scale.
A model that takes images (and often video) with text and produces text: descriptions, answers about charts and screenshots, visual reasoning.
A model that maps camera images and a language instruction to robot actions, extending vision-language models to control.
A learned model of how an environment evolves in response to actions, used for planning, imagination-based training or generated simulation.
Learning to choose actions to maximise cumulative reward through trial and feedback. Preference methods such as DPO are classified separately as preference optimization.
The algorithm that computes how each parameter contributed to the loss, so gradient descent can update it.
The European Union's risk-based regulation of AI systems, Regulation (EU) 2024/1689. Application dates are phased; verify the current timetable.
An open standard for cryptographically signed provenance metadata describing how media was made and edited, including AI generation.
Research that tries to explain model behaviour by analysing internal components such as features and circuits.
An open-source LLM serving engine known for paged KV-cache memory and continuous batching.
A C/C++ inference engine for running quantised models on CPUs and consumer GPUs using the GGUF format.
Recording prompts, retrieved context, tool calls, outputs, latency and cost to debug and improve AI applications, while protecting sensitive data in those records.
